prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength trapping concept to the demonstration of fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: After reading all eight ballots I move optical lattice clocks (B001) from second to first place. It is the only shortlisted candidate that eight of eight members ranked, with three first places and my own rank 2, and the support comes from atomic physics, condensed matter, statistical physics, materials and astroparticle members alike, so it does not depend on one subfield's enthusiasm. The scientific case is strong: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice made it possible to interrogate many atoms with negligible trap-induced shifts, and Ye's group turned that into clocks with systematic uncertainty near 1e-18 and many-body coherence, which is what now supports relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, tests of constant variation and dark-matter searches. Both names are clearly decisive, so a two-person prize needs no awkward cut. It has been independently reproduced at several national laboratories and compared across continents.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: Hall and Haensch (frequency combs, 2005) and Wineland (single-ion clocks, 2012) laid much of the technical ground, and a committee could view lattice clocks as the natural continuation of that line rather than a distinct discovery. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so some of the societal payoff is prospective. Credit is also not perfectly clean, since Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and other lattice-clock groups contributed and are outside the credited names. I judge these points as real but insufficient to outweigh the confirmation and breadth of the work.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first on the strength of Katori's idea and the atomic-structure control behind 1e-18 accuracy, but asks whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I do not think we should wait. The discovery is the lattice clock and its demonstrated accuracy, and that stands independently of the metrology bodies' schedule. Tying the prize to an SI decision would make our judgment depend on a process outside physics. Your own point that polarisabilities and blackbody and relativistic shifts had to be controlled so carefully is, to me, the scientific core that justifies the award, and I would put it in the citation language rather than the redefinition.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B001 first but notes that some members may see it as incremental after the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I share the concern but come out differently. The 2005 prize gave the comb as the clockwork and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions; neither introduced state-insensitive trapping of thousands of neutral atoms, which is what moved the stability limit by orders of magnitude. I would resist, however, your suggestion that Zoller and Cirac can be assumed covered in the trapped-ion entry elsewhere in your ranking: that is a separate argument I do not need for this prize.

responses.point: Pearce ranks topological insulators (B024) first with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a coherent theory-plus-experiment trio, and ranks circuit QED last partly because of the recent 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the cleanest three from the supplied names and I keep B024 as an alternative. My reservation is that Hasan's 3D work and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction fall outside this configuration, so the prize would leave out people many in the field regard as decisive, which makes it harder to defend than the clock prize. On your point about the 2025 prize and circuit QED I largely concede: I ranked cQED first, but its overlap with the 2025 recognition of circuits, together with my own position, is a reason for me not to press it.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B013) first as the most convincing theory-plus-experiment story, with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as the core and Andrei's role the hard question.
responses.response: Of the candidates I ranked lower, B013 has the most support and I take your argument seriously; it is why I place it among my alternatives. My hesitation is maturity rather than originality: the flat-band prediction and the 2018 discovery are secure, but the pairing mechanism is open and the field is eight years old. I also think the Andrei question is more than an allocation detail, because her STM evidence predates the transport discovery, and a three-person limit forces a choice that I am not convinced is fair. I would be willing to revisit this if you or Mehlig argue that the correlated-insulator physics is now settled enough.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
How to treat Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and other lattice-clock groups outside the credited names.

Whether the maturity concerns about magic-angle graphene (pairing mechanism, Andrei attribution) will resolve in its favour by a later round, which would make it a stronger first choice than I currently judge.
statement.conflict_note: Circuit QED (B029), my own opening first choice, falls squarely within my research and my role as director of WACQT at Chalmers, where Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson are colleagues, Anton Frisk Kockum is a frequent co-author, and several researchers associated with the 2025 prize have visited; I should recuse myself from any decision on B029 and have discounted it here. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for optical lattice clocks (B001), topological insulators (B024) or twisted bilayer graphene (B013).
